How Many Parameters the Objective Takes

Source: R/starters.R
infer_npar.Rd

Determines the length of the parameter vector by trying lengths and recording which ones the objective accepts. minimize() calls it when a starter was given without npar and the bounds do not determine it.

Usage

infer_npar(fn, gr, probe, npar_max = 50)

Arguments

fn

The objective.

gr

Its gradient, or NULL. Supplying one makes the answer much more likely to be unique; see Details.

probe

A function of one integer returning a candidate parameter vector of that length, so that the objective is probed where it will be used.

npar_max

The largest length tried. Defaults to 50.

Value

A single integer, the one length that is accepted. Signals an error that names the first two lengths found when more than one length is accepted, and an error when the search accepts no length.

Details

A length is accepted when fn returns a single finite number for it and raises neither an error nor a warning, and, if gr was supplied, when the gradient comes back with the same length as its argument.

The probe works when the objective rejects a wrong length, as the objective of a modeling package usually does: X %*% beta with a parameter of the wrong length is an error and not a number, so a regression model is settled at once. A gradient helps when it writes its components out, since such a gradient returns a fixed number of them, whatever its argument.

A vectorized objective written only in terms of the parameter vector behaves differently. Recycling warns only when the shorter length is not a divisor of the longer, so sum((p - c(1, 2, 3))^2) accepts a vector of length one without a warning and returns the finite value 14; and its gradient 2 * (p - c(1, 2, 3)) returns six components for an argument of length six, so the gradient test accepts that length too. The Rosenbrock function 100 (p_2 - p_1^2)^2 + (1 - p_1)^2, written with p[1] and p[2], accepts every length from two upwards for a related reason. The length cannot be determined from such an objective.

The probe therefore settles the objectives that have a fixed width built into them and rejects the others, with an error that names two lengths that were accepted. The caller then gives the count through npar or through a vector of bounds.

The search stops as soon as a second length is accepted, because the answer is then ambiguous. The cost is therefore two evaluations when the objective accepts any length, and npar_max when it accepts exactly one. Either way it happens once, before the run.

See also

start_zeros() and start_runif(), the starters that make this determination necessary, and minimize(), which calls it.

Examples

# A hand-written gradient pins it exactly.
f  <- function(p) 100 * (p[2] - p[1]^2)^2 + (1 - p[1])^2
gr <- function(p) c(-400 * p[1] * (p[2] - p[1]^2) - 2 * (1 - p[1]),
                    200 * (p[2] - p[1]^2))
infer_npar(f, gr, function(k) numeric(k))
#> [1] 2

# Without one, the same objective accepts any length from two upwards,
# and the error names the two lengths that were accepted first.
try(infer_npar(f, NULL, function(k) numeric(k)))
#> Error : The objective accepts more than one length of parameter vector (2 and 3),
#>   so the number of parameters cannot be worked out from it. Say how many,
#>   as in start_zeros(npar = 3).

# An objective with a fixed width is settled without a gradient, which is
# the ordinary case for a model.
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(40 * 3), 40, 3)
y <- as.numeric(X %*% c(1, -2, 0.5) + rnorm(40))
infer_npar(function(b) sum((y - X %*% b)^2), NULL, function(k) numeric(k))
#> [1] 3
